title: A Victory That Breaks David's Heart
overview: David's army defeats the revolt led by his son Absalom, but Absalom is killed against David's orders, and the king's grief overwhelms the news of victory.

parts.label: David sends out his army (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: David, who had fled east of the Jordan when his son Absalom seized power, splits his forces into three, and his men insist he stay in the city because losing him would mean losing everything. In front of the whole army he orders his commanders to treat Absalom gently, a father's plea in the middle of a war against that same son.

parts.label: Battle in the forest (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: "Israel" here means the people who followed Absalom, so this is a civil war, and the death toll is huge. Fleeing men were likely trapped by the dense woods and rough ground, so the forest itself killed more than the fighting did.

parts.label: Joab kills Absalom (vv. 9-15)
parts.note: Absalom's head gets caught in an oak's branches, perhaps by his famous long hair, and one soldier refuses any reward to kill him because the king forbade it. Joab, David's tough army chief, ignores the order and strikes, probably judging that the kingdom would never be safe while Absalom lived.

parts.label: A pit and a pile of stones (vv. 16-18)
parts.note: Joab stops the slaughter, and Absalom is thrown into a pit under a heap of stones, likely a sign of disgrace. The writer sets this beside the grand monument Absalom had built to keep his own name alive, since he had no son.

parts.label: Two runners with news (vv. 19-23)
parts.note: Ahimaaz, son of the priest Zadok, is eager to carry the news, but Joab holds him back, likely because bringing word of the king's son's death was dangerous and unwelcome. Joab sends a Cushite, a man from the region south of Egypt, but Ahimaaz insists on running too, goes by way of the plain and arrives first, though why that route was quicker is unclear.

parts.label: David hears and weeps (vv. 24-33)
parts.note: A man running alone usually meant a messenger rather than a fleeing army, so David hopes for good news, and Ahimaaz announces the win but dodges the question about Absalom. When the Cushite makes the death plain, David cries that he wishes he had died instead of his son, the father in him outweighing the king.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether David's mercy and grief toward Absalom are shown as a picture of deep love, which some Christians link to God's love for those who turn against him, or as a father's blindness that put his people and kingdom at risk.
think: When someone you love has done real harm, can grieving for them and judging what they did both be true at the same time?
